proposedDescription: A patch of white, wool-like wax on a pine twig may be hiding these tiny insects. Pineus boerneri is an adelgid, a close relative of aphids that feeds on pine trees. Its young crawl to new feeding sites, while the settled insects and eggs shelter beneath the wax. Heavy infestations can yellow needles and damage shoots. Other pine adelgids look very similar, so identifying the insect takes more than recognizing its white covering.
researchNotes: Gap resolved with two independent field studies from Colombia and Brazil, read as full PDFs. Both support pine feeding, wax-covered colonies and tree damage. Development times vary with conditions and are not generalized. Species confirmation requires insect characters, not wax alone.

It grows close to the ground or rises on spreading branches, with narrow leaves and small greenish flowers gathered at the ends of its stems. The tiny fruits have a rough, wrinkled surface, a useful detail for distinguishing it from other amaranths. Look for this inconspicuous herb in disturbed ground, including paths, gardens and vacant lots, where its flowers can easily blend into the surrounding greenery.

proposedDescription: Orange-yellow patches on the undersides of alder leaves can be signs of this rust fungus. Infected leaves may develop spots, curl, brown and fall early, leaving heavily affected trees with thin crowns. Melampsoridium hiratsukanum produces spores that can travel through the air, and its full life cycle includes both alder and larch. Other rust fungi can cause similar symptoms, so leaf damage alone is not enough to identify it; specialists examine spores and may use DNA testing.

proposedDescription: Alfalfa is familiar as a forage crop, but it can also persist outside cultivated fields. In its South American home it is a familiar colonizer of open places, and it can also establish beyond its native range. Researchers have found self-sustaining stands along waterways and disturbed ground in parts of Southeast Asia. Closely related Cecropia species can look alike, making careful identification important when documenting new records.
